1:
Masters, or teachers? Most read it of the teaching office. Gill takes it as a rebuke to the Jewish affectation of being called Rabbi and advises men rather to be hearers, though the office is a good work. Ellicott renders it teachers and aims the condemnation at those who appoint themselves and are as blind leaders of the blind. Robertson translates it as a prohibition already in progress — stop becoming many teachers — and reads a complaint that too many were teaching what they did not comprehend. Barnes makes this desire the key to the whole chapter, which otherwise has no evident connection with its surroundings. Wesley compresses it: let no more take this upon you than God thrusts out.

Calvin dissents from what he calls the common and almost universal interpretation. He takes masters not as those who performed a public duty in the Church, but as such as took upon them the right of passing judgment on others — and supports it from usage, since among Greeks and Latins those were called masters who superciliously animadverted on others. His reason for the plural is memorable: many everywhere did thrust themselves in, for it is an innate disease in mankind to seek reputation by blaming others. He is careful that this does not forbid brotherly admonition, only that immoderate desire to condemn which proceeds from ambition and pride, when a man slanders, carps, bites, and seeks what he may turn to a sinister purpose. Henry stands nearer Calvin: do not give yourselves the air of teachers, imposers and judges, nor make your own sentiments the standard for all others.

On the greater judgment they agree, pressing it differently. Calvin makes it exact retribution: he imposes a hard law on himself who tries others by the rule of extreme rigor, nor does he deserve pardon who will pardon none. Robertson gives the plain reason: the pretence of knowledge adds to the teacher’s responsibility and condemnation. Clarke is blunter about the men he has in view, who undertake to show us the way of salvation, know nothing of it, and are unsaved themselves. His verdict: blockheads are common, and knaves and hypocrites may be found everywhere.

Then the quarrel this chapter is famous for. Gill reads we all offend as universal: no man lives without sin, there is sin in a good man’s holy things, and no man is perfect in this life. Clarke calls that a very bad and dangerous doctrine which, pushed to its consequences, would greatly affect the credibility of the whole Gospel system — and answers by reductio. James includes himself after the common manner of teachers; press that literally and he was one of the many teachers who receive the greater condemnation, that he was a horse-breaker because he says we put bits in the horses’ mouths, and that his tongue was a world of iniquity set on fire of hell. No man of even tolerable morals could be guilty of those things. Wesley takes the same side: doubtless some are able to bridle the whole body, and so are in this sense perfect.

What then is the perfect man? Barnes keeps it modest: not spotless, but in complete control of himself, as a man governs a horse by the bit. Ellicott adds why the sign is reliable: not that stilling the tongue quiets every other member, but that the work of ruling the one rebel is so great that a much less effort keeps the rest in subjection. Robertson notices that the word is husband as well as man, and draws the domestic inference: the wife is at liberty to test her husband by this rule of the tongue. Calvin ends on the censors: they pretended a zeal for perfect holiness but ought to have begun with the tongue, and since they made no account of bridling it they exhibited only a fictitious sanctity.
3:
Ellicott supplies the frame: three comparisons are introduced here, the bit, the rudder and a fire, the two former to show what mastery may be gained by self-discipline, the latter to warn of a danger which may quickly spread beyond our power to quell. He also pauses to be rude about a variant, whose supporters argue that the least likely reading is the most so — making every slip of a copyist more sacred in their eyes than the received text is to believers in verbal inspiration.

On the bit the point is the disproportion. Gill observes that horses are without understanding, need direction, and are strong, and would be ungovernable unless bits were put in their mouths. Calvin puts it more sharply: though a horse be a ferocious animal, he is turned about at the will of his rider because he is bridled — and no less can the tongue serve to govern a man. Barnes draws the conclusion the apostle wants: he who has proper control of his tongue can govern his whole body, as the man who holds a bridle turns about the horse.

The ship adds the wind. Barnes thinks the fierce winds are not decoration: by them the apostle probably meant the power of the passions, so that even a man under impetuous passion would be restrained if the tongue were controlled, as a driven ship is by the helm. He adds that the ancient rudder was shaped like an oar, and so was very small compared with the vessel — about as small as the tongue is compared with the body. Ellicott hears the writer’s own weather in the simile, remembering the storms of the Galilean lake, though he may have known only the craft of an inland sea; and none knew better than the brother of the Lord who was the true Helm of the ships that keep pathway along the deep. Robertson brings it forward: if James had only seen the modern mammoth ships — though the ship on which Paul went to Malta carried two hundred and seventy-six persons — and the word for the steersman would today apply to the chauffeur. He quotes the judgment that there is more imagery drawn from natural phenomena in this one short epistle than in all of Paul’s put together.

What does the little member boast? Clarke hears the Greek orators, whose all-commanding eloquence could carry the great mob whithersoever they wished, calming them to submission or exciting them to furious sedition — and he takes boasting to mean simply that the tongue can do great things, of a good or an evil kind. Calvin makes the same correction explicitly: James did not intend to reprove ostentation so much as to show that the tongue is the doer of great things, since vain boasting is not suitable to the bridle and the helm. Barnes keeps a little of the boast: the tongue seems conscious of its power and boasts largely, but not unjustly. Wesley gives the whole clause three words: hath great influence.

Then the fire, where the translation is disputed. Barnes notes the Greek means a wood, a forest, then fire-wood, so a very little fire suffices to ignite a great quantity of combustible material — a spark will kindle a lofty pile, and a word may set a village in a flame. Ellicott would render it outright as how great a forest a little spark kindleth, as the Latin has it and our own margin allows; he thinks the writer had in mind the wrapping of some vast forest in flame by the falling of a single spark. Robertson finds the same in the grammar, two indirect questions of the same form standing together — what-sized fire kindles what-sized forest? — and adds that forest fires were common in ancient times as now, and were usually caused by small sparks carelessly thrown.
6:
Gill alone begins with what fire is good for: it is useful in its place, to warm and comfort, and so is the tongue in Christian conversation and in the ministry of the word, where the hearts of God’s children burn while the Scriptures are opened. But fire should be watched: as it kindles into a flame, so unchaste and angry words stir up the flame of lust, envy and revenge; and what wood is to fire, that are whisperers, tale-bearers and backbiters.

What is a world of iniquity? Barnes takes it as a little world of evil in itself, as we speak of a town as a world in miniature, so that all the kinds of evil in the world are exhibited there in little — and he runs the list out: who can measure the evils arising from scandal, slander, perjury, blasphemy and obscenity, or number the broils, contentions and wars which the tongue produces? If all men were dumb, what a portion of the crimes of the world would cease. Clarke treats it as an idiom rather than a doctrine: world signifies a mass, a great collection, as we say a world of troubles, or as one lexicographer called his own book a world of words; the Latins said an ocean of evils. Calvin reaches it by another image: to call it a world is the same as calling it the sea or the abyss — a slender portion of flesh contains in it the whole world of iniquity.

Clarke brings two rabbinic sayings, the strangest thing in the chapter. In the first, man is said to have a hundred and forty-eight members, some confined and others free, the tongue placed between the jaws. Come and see what a flame the tongue kindles — were it an unconfined member, what would it not do? In the second, God says to the tongue: all the rest of the members are erect, but thou liest down; all are external, but thou art internal. Nor is this enough: I have built two walls about thee, the one bone, the other flesh.

The wheel of nature defeats them. Robertson quotes the verdict that this is one of the hardest passages in the Bible, and finds it impossible as it stands, suggesting the comma may belong after fire rather than iniquity. He allows that the wheel of birth was a current phrase, used physiologically or philosophically, and the writer may have caught the metaphor from that use — but certainly he has no Orphic or Pythagorean doctrine of the transmigration of souls; and there is no reference to the zodiac. Calvin offers two readings: either human life is compared to a course or wheel, or the word means a violent impulse, since we call that fervid which is accompanied with violence — on which reading the tongue is like untamed horses, which draw the chariots violently and hurry a man headlong. He rejects the whole course of life as conveying no idea, and takes it as the whole machinery of our nature, every faculty belonging to man. Wesley says it in six words: all the passions, every wheel of his soul.

Ellicott sorts the temptations. Three to smite with the tongue are specially powerful of evil — as relief from passion, as gratification of spite, and as revenge for wrong; the first experienced by hot-tempered folk, the second yielded to by the malicious, the third welcomed by the weak and defenceless — and all of us at times are in each of these divisions. He wants the Jewish name for the place of torment kept in the last clause, whence the rich man of the parable begged water to cool his tongue. Calvin takes the same clause as a definition: the outrageousness of the tongue is the flame of the infernal fire, and a bad tongue is the organ of the devil.
7:
Barnes takes the claim about taming seriously enough to check it. Nearly all the beasts we call domestic, and see only when tame, were once fierce and savage races — the horse, the ox, the ass, the swine, the dog, the cat. He quotes an authority that there is perhaps no creature to which man has access which might not be tamed with proper perseverance, and that the ancients made more exertions to this end, and with better success, than ourselves: the examples on record run to elephants, lions and tigers, the eagle, asps and other serpents, crocodiles and fishes; the lion was commonly tamed by the ancient Egyptians and trained to assist in hunting and in war. The one animal supposed to have defied man is the hyena, and even that has been subdued in modern times.

Clarke has something better than authorities — a witness. He reports credible information, received when he was in the Zetland Isles, of seals being domesticated, and of one that would pass part of his time on shore, take his milk from the servants, go again to sea, and return. Ellicott takes the same fact devotionally: all kinds have been mastered by mankind, and there lives no creature which may not be won by kindness; he ends with the verse about him who prayeth best who loveth best all things great and small. Robertson works from the two tenses: the present gives the continuous process, through the ages, of man’s lordship over the animals, the perfect the state of conquest already achieved in some cases.

Calvin uses the taming as a proof. There is no animal so savage which is not tamed by the skill of man: fishes, which in a manner inhabit another world; birds, so quick and roving; serpents, so inimical to mankind. Since then the tongue cannot be restrained, there must be some secret fire of hell hidden in it. He is careful about the scope: what is said of wild beasts and serpents is not to be understood of them all, and it is enough that man should subdue some of the most ferocious. Wesley disposes of the difficulty in a clause: the expression perhaps is not to be taken strictly.

Then no man can tame the tongue — and every one of them qualifies it. Barnes: not that it is never brought under control, but that it is impossible effectually and certainly to subdue it. Ellicott: the writer does not mean that no one can tame his own tongue, for then he would hardly be responsible for its vagaries, and it is written later that these things ought not so to be. Robertson: especially his own tongue, and by himself — but one has the help of the Holy Spirit. Wesley: of another, no, nor his own, without peculiar help from God. Gill spells it out: no man can by his own power tame his tongue, though God by his Spirit and grace can and often does change the note of the curser, swearer, liar and blasphemer. Clarke’s version is the grimmest: nothing but the grace of God, excision, or death can bring it under subjection.

The deadly poison draws out the strongest writing in the chapter. Barnes says no sting of a serpent does so much evil in the world, and asks who can stand before the slanderer — then quotes the playwright: slander, whose edge is sharper than the sword, whose tongue outvenoms all the worms of Nile, whose breath rides on the posting winds and doth belie all corners of the world. Clarke says the description must have the slanderer, calumniator, backbiter and tale-bearer in view, and that vipers, basilisks and rattlesnakes are not more dangerous to life than these are to the peace and reputation of men. Robertson gives it the last image: like the restless death-bringing tongue of the asp before it strikes.
9:
Clarke tells the best story in the chapter, from the rabbis. A master sent his servant to bring good food from the market, and the servant bought tongues; sent later for bad food, he again bought tongues. Asked why, he answered that from the tongue both good and evil come to man: if it be good, there is nothing better; if bad, there is nothing worse. Clarke pairs it with a second saying: the mouth desires to study in the law and to praise God with hymns, but it can also slander, blaspheme, reproach and swear falsely. Gill states the objection plainly: it is not only a contradiction, but unnatural, as well as wicked and sinful. Then his own experience: to find a man who officiates in sacred things to be a common swearer is truly monstrous, but he has known several.

Three of them independently take up the objection that the image is gone. Calvin states it: were any one to say that the image of God has been blotted out by the sin of Adam, we must confess it has been miserably deformed, but in such a way that some of its lineaments still appear — righteousness and the freedom of choosing good have been lost, but many excellent endowments by which we excel the brutes still remain. Wesley reaches the same in one sentence: we have now lost this likeness, yet there remains from thence an indelible nobleness, which we ought to reverence both in ourselves and others. Ellicott is severest about the consequence: the likeness of God assuredly remains in the most abandoned and fallen, and to curse it is to invoke the wrath of its Creator — what then can be urged in defence of the anathemas and fulminations of councils, or the mutual execrations of sects and schisms?

Ellicott hears something in the mildness of the rebuke. The Greek behind ought not is found only here in the New Testament and seems strangely weak when we reflect on the usual vehemence of the writer — was he sadly conscious of the failure beforehand of his protest? At least there seems no trace of satire in the sorrowful cadence of his line, out of the same mouth. Robertson confirms it grammatically: the only use of that old impersonal verb in the New Testament, more like saying a thing is not appropriate than that it is not permitted; and the infinitive means not merely so to be, but so to keep on happening.

The fountain gets a location. Ellicott takes it for a vivid picture, probably, of the mineral springs abounding in the Jordan valley near the Dead Sea, contrasted with the clear and sparkling rivulets of the north, fed by the snows of Lebanon; nature had no confusion in her plans. Barnes notes the word means an opening or fissure, such as there is in rocks from which a fountain gushes, and that such things do not occur in nature and should not be found in man.

The last clause is disputed. Clarke reports that the received reading, that no fountain can yield salt water and fresh, is absent from several old manuscripts and versions, which give instead, neither can salt water produce sweet — a reading one critic called undoubtedly genuine. On that reading, he says, there are four distinct comparisons rather than three, the last being that salt water cannot be made sweet. Calvin knows the same variant. Ellicott takes the disputed clause as saying that salt water cannot bring forth fresh, and quotes the application: if the mouth emit cursing, thereby making itself a brackish spring, it cannot also emit the sweet stream of praise; if it appear to do so, all must be hypocrisy and mere seeming. Clarke ends drily — according to the ordinary operations of nature these things are impossible, and chemical analysis is out of the question.
13:
Gill sets the entrance requirement: the first lesson in the school of spiritual wisdom is that a man know he is a fool. Henry insists on two things together: a truly wise man will not set up for the reputation of being wise without a good stock of knowledge, nor value himself on knowing things if he has not wisdom to apply them; true wisdom does not lie in good notions so much as in good and useful actions, and neither he who thinks well nor he who talks well is wise if he does not live well.

On meekness the images are better than the arguments. Barnes observes that the truly wise man is always characterized by a calm spirit and mild demeanour, and that a noisy, boisterous and stormy declaimer we never select as a safe counsellor. Clarke is harder on the learned: proud and disdainful men who pass for great scholars may have learning but not wisdom, and are like the blind man who carried a lantern in daylight to keep others from jostling him in the street. That learning is not only little worth but despicable which does not teach a man to govern his own spirit. Robertson calls meekness of wisdom a startling combination, and adds that actions speak louder than words even in the professional wise man. Ellicott traces the word we render conversation: literally a turning of oneself about, it became walking to and fro, then the talking done while so walking, and at last its narrow modern use.

What is bitter envying? Ellicott would read bitter zeal and party-spirit, and gives the word its local history: that zeal had caused Jerusalem to run with blood, and the Zealots were really assassins, pledged to any iniquity — such were the forty who bound themselves under a curse to neither eat nor drink till they had killed Paul. Some of these desperadoes escaped the Romans and fled to Mount Lebanon, where they were probably the nucleus of the medieval society of the Old Man of the Mountain; our word assassin comes from the name of their first sheik. Wesley answers in a line what true zeal is: the flame of love. Calvin finds the root in pride: it is usual with hypocrites to exalt themselves by criminating all others, as was formerly the case with many philosophers, who sought glory by a bitter abuse of all other orders.

Clarke turns the verse on the controversialists and quotes a poet at them: be calm in arguing, for fierceness makes error a fault and truth discourtesy; why should I feel another man’s mistakes more than his sickness or his poverty? In love I should; but anger is not love, nor wisdom neither. Let all writers on what is called polemic divinity, he says — glossing the word as fighting, warring — lay this to heart: if you are under an unkind and contemptuous spirit even while pretending to defend true religion, do not boast of your success in silencing an adversary.

The three adjectives are read as a descending scale. Calvin says earthly, sensual and devilish are directly contrary to heavenly, spiritual and divine, and that a man following his own mind without the Spirit soon becomes a prey to the delusions of Satan. Barnes concedes that the wisdom denied here is real ability — in the contentions of church and state, at the bar and in theological disputes, there is often learning, shrewdness, tact and skilful argumentation, making the worse appear the better reason, yet joined to a spirit so narrow as to show it had no origin in heaven. On the confusion that follows: where this spirit prevails in a church it is impossible to expect progress in divine things, and any effort to do good is vain — the Spirit, like a peaceful dove, flies from the realms of noise and strife.
17:
Two of them read the order of the words in opposite ways. Barnes insists the passage is about persons, not propositions, and should not be applied, as it often is, to doctrine, as though a church ought to be first pure and then peaceable in what it believes; the first effect of religion is not on the intellect but on the heart, to make the man upright and good. He then charges the misreading with a history: most of the persecutions in the church have grown out of that maxim, which led to the establishment of the Inquisition and kindled the fires of Smithfield; a pure spirit is the best promoter of peace, and does more than anything else to secure the prevalence of truth. Robertson takes the other side: great as peace is, purity comes before peace, and peace at any price is not worth the having — hence Jesus spurned the devil’s peace of surrender.

On the catalogue itself Clarke is the most useful, glossing each term: chaste and clean; promoting peace among men; meek, of an equal mind, taking everything in good part and putting the best construction on the actions of others; not stubborn, of a yielding disposition in all indifferent things; rendering to every man his due, never swayed by self-interest or the fear of man; and, last, without dissimulation, never working under a mask. Wesley compresses the same into single words: soft, mild, yielding, not rigid; frank, open. Ellicott sets the catalogue against the foulness before it, compares it with the fruits of the Spirit, and adds that this wisdom cannot be gotten for gold, neither shall silver be weighed for the price thereof.

One word in the list divides them. Calvin reports that it occurs only here, and has been variously rendered because the verb behind it can mean to discern, to judge, to examine, to contend, or to doubt: hence uncensorious, incontroversial, impartial, and not doubting. He prefers uncensorious, glossing it as excluding that over-anxious inquiry of hypocrites, who too minutely examine the sayings and doings of their brethren and put on them the worst construction. Robertson takes the reading Calvin lists last and makes it decisive: the word means unhesitating, not doubting like the man earlier in the epistle — this wisdom does not put a premium on doubt.

Clarke supplies the background: the wisdom from above is greatly celebrated among the rabbis as the supernal wisdom, taken for a peculiar inspiration of the Almighty, or a teaching communicated by the angels — one saying has it that this wisdom was in Adam more than in the supreme angels, and he knew all things; another that angels were sent from heaven and taught it to Enoch. Gill makes a claim of his own on the name: those possessed of this wisdom are the only true Gnostics. But its properties, Clarke adds, are not found in such detail in any rabbinical writer.

The closing image is agricultural, and Barnes lingers on it. The farmer sows his seed in peace; the fields are not sown amidst the tumults of a mob, and nothing is more calm than the farmer walking with measured tread over his fields scattering his seed — so the seed of the kingdom is scattered by noiseless and unobtrusive labourers. Calvin guards against the obvious abuse, that peaceableness must mean covering vices: those wise according to God’s will are so kind as yet not to favour vices, but strive to correct them in moderation — those who wish to be physicians to heal vices ought not to be executioners. Clarke offers another rendering of the obscure line, that the peaceable fruits of righteousness are sown for the practisers of peace, so that he who labours to live peaceably shall have peace for his reward. Robertson ends it in eight words: only those who act peaceably are entitled to peace.
